back: A practice: everyone merges small changes into the shared mainline at least daily, and every merge is automatically built and tested.
Delivery: every passing change is releasable with one action; a human chooses when. Deployment: every passing change goes to production automatically.
An automated sequence of stages each commit passes through, cheapest first; a failure at any stage stops the change.

front: Time budget for the commit stage?
back: Under about 10 minutes, so developers wait for the result instead of starting the next task and batching changes.
Deployment frequency, lead time for changes, change failure rate, and time to restore service.
Everyone merges into one main branch at least daily, via branches that live hours not weeks; unfinished work hides behind feature flags.
Many fast unit tests, fewer integration tests, very few end-to-end tests. The inverted version is the ice-cream cone anti-pattern.

front: 200 tests, each 0.5% flaky. Chance the suite is green?
back: 0.995^200 ≈ e^-1 ≈ 37%. So 63% of runs fail with no real bug.
A consumer publishes what it expects from a provider's API; the provider's pipeline verifies every published contract still holds. Pact is the well-known tool.

front: What to do with a flaky test?
back: Quarantine it out of the blocking path with an owner and deadline, fix the cause, and push the check down the pyramid. Do not just add retries.
Build one immutable artifact per commit and promote the same bytes through every environment, changing only config.
A tag (api:prod) is a mutable pointer that can move. A digest (sha256:…) is the content hash and always means the same bytes. Deploy by digest.

front: Why use OIDC federation in CI?
back: The job exchanges a signed identity token for short-lived cloud credentials, so no long-lived keys sit in CI secrets to be stolen.
Roll back: redeploy the previous artifact (fast, if compatible). Roll forward: ship a fix through the pipeline (needed when rollback is unsafe).
Changes the old code cannot handle: a dropped or renamed column, a new message or cache format, or side effects like emails and payments.
Scales the Deployment's previous ReplicaSet revision back up. Kubernetes keeps revisionHistoryLimit old revisions, 10 by default.
